source: Kenett, Anaki and Faust (2014) Investigating the structure of semantic networks in low and high creative persons
finding: Group free-association networks of high-creative people (HSC) have shorter paths, smaller diameter and more small-world structure than low-creative (LSC). Groups were made by a decision tree on RAT using tertiles.
numbers: 144 recruited, 139 kept (47 men, 92 women). Free association on 33 per group, 96 target words, 1 min each. RAT mean LSC 7 (SD 2.7) vs HSC 13.2 (SD 3). ASPL 4.6 vs 3.93; diameter 12 vs 8; small-world S 6.86 vs 7.76; modularity 0.62 vs 0.58; clustering 0.67 vs 0.66 (all unweighted PMFG). Bootstrap half-node samples p<0.001 but differences tiny (Q 0.55 vs 0.54). HSC gave more unique responses, F(1,191)=310.9.
quote: The semantic memory network of persons with low creative ability seems to be more rigid, compared to the network of persons with high creative ability
limits: Networks are per group, not per person. Only 96 words, one Hebrew sample, extreme-group (tertile) design. Authors say modularity gap is small and may reflect network size. HSC give more associations, so fluency is a confound. Not preregistered. Metaphor accuracy gap only p<0.08.
agent_relevance: Founding result, but the sample behind the small effect is 33 per group and the clustering gap is 0.01. Treat it as a hypothesis for seed distance in O7, not a settled law.

source: Kenett, Anaki and Faust (2014) - first-10-response control
finding: When only the first 10 responses per cue are used to control for fluency, LSC is still less connected, more spread out and less small-world, but the modularity effect reverses.
numbers: Node impact: Mann-Whitney U=3523, p<0.005; positive-impact nodes 44% of LSC vs 65% of HSC. Unique responses significant for 60% of target words.
limits: Reversal of modularity under the fluency control means one of the four headline metrics is not robust. Authors flag this themselves.
agent_relevance: Path-length and spread effects survive a fluency control; the modularity claim does not. Our agent should key on path length and reach, not on modularity.

source: Kenett et al. (2018) Flexibility of thought in high creative individuals represented by percolation analysis, PNAS
finding: Same 33 LSC and 33 HSC data re-analysed with percolation. HSC network holds together longer when weak links are removed, so it is more flexible and robust.
numbers: 140 recruited, 33 per group, 96 cues. Percolation integral LSC 14.76 vs HSC 15.64. Noise SD 0.0001 t=-2790.59; SD 0.01 15.10 vs 15.81, t=-59.35. Link shuffle reverses sign (21.45 vs 20.55), so effect comes from structure. HSC interlinks 0.04 vs LSC 0.03; intralinks no difference. 21 of 28 matched interlinks (75%) stronger in HSC. Component overlap about 87%.
limits: Same dataset as 2014, so not an independent replication. Authors admit only initial insight, creativity treated as binary, group-level networks, inconsistent link counts (4000 vs 4500), HSC weights rescaled by 1.3 for fluency.
agent_relevance: Suggests creative memory has more bridges between clusters. For the agent: seed from two different clusters (bridges) rather than just far words.

source: Brain connectivity-based prediction of real-life creativity is mediated by semantic memory structure, Science Advances
finding: In an individual-level network study, more creative people (real-life creative activity and achievement) have LESS modular semantic networks, a partial independent confirmation of the flexibility idea.
numbers: 94 behaviour, 93 fMRI, 35 cues, 595 pairs rated. Spearman after FDR: weighted ASPL vs C-Act rs=-0.276 (p=.007); weighted Q vs C-Ach rs=-0.295 (p=.004); unweighted Q vs C-Act rs=-0.281, vs C-Ach rs=-0.287. Mediation indirect effects significant (e.g. 0.135 [0.024,0.320]), direct effects not.
limits: Sample about 94, no external validation. Resting-state check failed for unweighted modularity (rs=0.103, p=.327). One word set, one relatedness task. Correlations of about 0.28 mean roughly 8% variance.
agent_relevance: Real independent-sample support (individual networks, different language, real-life creativity) but small, about r=0.28. Supports the direction, not a strong dial.

source: Brain connectivity-based prediction - note on direction of effect
finding: The direction is shorter-path and lower-modularity for creative people, but the effect is on modularity of ratings of pairs, not path length in free association, so the two kinds of network are not the same measurement.
numbers: UUN ASPL mean 1.633 (SD 0.221); WUN Q mean 0.122 (SD 0.058); C-Act mean 47.9 (SD 21.7); C-Ach mean 74.6 (SD 42.2).
limits: Different network method (relatedness judgment, not free association), so this is a conceptual replication only.
agent_relevance: Conclusion should not depend on one way of building the network; the agent should not assume one specific graph measure.

source: Anon (2022) An investigation of the cognitive and neural correlates of semantic memory search related to creative ability, Communications Biology
finding: Clustering in verbal search predicts divergent thinking output; switching does not. Switching links to network global efficiency and executive tests. Mixed picture for the idea that search structure, not distance, drives creativity.
numbers: 86 French speakers. PolyFT PCA: clustering 52% and switching 31% of variance. Clustering vs AUT fluency and uniqueness p<0.001 (survive FDR), commonness p=0.013. Switching vs AUT: none. Switching vs global efficiency p=0.007 unweighted (FDR). Switching vs CAT accuracy p=0.032. Connectome prediction r=0.367 (clustering), 0.400 (switching).
limits: Small N, only three cue words, thresholded unweighted networks, some correlations did not survive correction.
agent_relevance: Staying inside a cluster (depth) predicted more and rarer ideas here, not jumping. Argues for depth-then-switch, not only far seeds.

source: Anon (2024) Creative connections: the neural correlates of semantic relatedness are associated with creativity, Communications Biology
finding: More creative people judge words as more related, and show less brain activity in default-mode and semantic-control regions as distance grows. Creative people may find links with less effort.
numbers: N=93 fMRI, 595 pairs, 35 cues. Rating falls with distance, Kendall tau=-0.56. Default-mode activity rises with distance tau=0.24. Mean RJT rating vs brain activity r=-0.41 p<0.001; C-Ach r=-0.24 p=0.046; AUT frequency r=0.28 p=0.022.
limits: Fixed trial order, difficulty confounded with relatedness, unbalanced trials per step, correlational, same sample as the Science Advances study.
agent_relevance: Suggests creative people lower the cost of linking distant concepts, so the lever is cheaper bridges, not farther seeds.

source: Montessori study (2021) Education shapes the structure of semantic memory and impacts creative thinking, npj Science of Learning
finding: Montessori children show slightly shorter paths, lower modularity and more creativity than traditionally schooled children, but network gaps are tiny. Quasi-experimental evidence that structure can differ by training.
numbers: 67 children (36 Montessori, 31 traditional), mean age 9.31. Networks 68 nodes, 198 edges. CC 0.707 vs 0.701 (d=0.51); ASPL 3.07 vs 3.12 (d=0.24); Q 0.582 vs 0.589 (d=0.32). Divergent creativity 9.6 vs 7.1 (d=0.58); convergent 5.3 vs 2.6 (d=1.74). Verbal fluency total 16.4 vs 14.8 (p=.225, d=0.30).
limits: Cross-sectional, one category (animals), 1000-resample bootstrap p-values inflate significance for 0.05-point gaps, not preregistered, data not public, text/table inconsistencies. Not causal.
agent_relevance: Network gaps of 0.05 on path length are far smaller than creativity gaps. A weak mediator at best; do not rely on it.

source: Domanti, Campidelli, Agnoli and De Angeli (2026) Are semantic networks associated with idea originality in artificial creativity? Comparison with human agents
finding: ChatGPT-4o has a longer-path, more modular, less clustered network than both high- and low-creative humans, and its network breaks apart faster under percolation. Yet its AUT ideas are more original than the low-creative humans'.
numbers: 81 psychology students (median split HCH/LCH) vs 81 GPT-4o chats. ASPL: GPT 4.378 vs LCH 3.429 vs HCH 3.325 (GPT-HCH d=2.55; LCH-HCH d=0.42). CC 0.705 vs 0.710 vs 0.715. Q 0.692 vs 0.666 vs 0.662. Percolation integral GPT 77.9, LCH 85.2, HCH 85.8 (F(2,977)=2544). Originality peaks: GPT 2.25, LCH 2.00, HCH 2.59. Fluency: GPT more than double humans (F(2,159)=438).
limits: One chat model (web interface, hyperparameters unknown), one task battery, tiny human sample, GPT originality had too little spread for a median split, networks built from different prompts so path length partly reflects fluency/format.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM test: network rigidity did not stop high AUT originality. For our agent, structure is not the bottleneck; selection and combination probably are.

source: Domanti et al. (2026) - literature table on LLM vs human creativity
finding: The paper tabulates peer-reviewed LLM-vs-human AUT studies: results are mixed. Some find LLMs equal to humans (9% of humans above LLMs), some find LLMs higher in originality and flexibility.
numbers: Examples: 100 humans vs 6 chatbots, LLMs equal to humans; 256 humans vs 3 chatbots, semantic distance LLM > human; 151 humans vs GPT-4 on AUT, DAT, TTCT, LLM > human originality; 42 students vs chatbots, humans > LLM in originality.
limits: A secondary table inside one paper; not independently checked against each primary.
agent_relevance: The 'LLMs are less distant than humans' claim is not settled; results depend on prompt and scorer.

source: Domanti et al. (2026) - citation of Wang et al. (2025) on LLM semantic fluency networks
finding: Reported secondhand: Wang et al. found LLM animal-fluency networks have higher ASPL, lower clustering and higher modularity than humans (30 humans, LLMs role-playing 30 occupations; GPT-3.5, GPT-4, several LLaMA).
numbers: Humans: 30 participants from a semantic fluency database. LLM role prompts: 30 occupations.
quote: LLMs have poorer creativity and flexibility compared to humans
limits: Not opened. Wang et al. did not measure creativity at all, so the conclusion is an inference from network shape. Role-play prompting was used to add diversity.
agent_relevance: Same direction as b09. Both claim LLM networks are rigid but neither tests whether that causes weaker ideas.

source: Chen and Ding (2023) Probing the Creativity of Large Language Models: Can Models Produce Divergent Semantic Association?
finding: On the Divergent Association Task (semantic distance between 10 unrelated nouns), GPT-4 beats most humans with greedy decoding. Temperature raises scores for other models but costs stability.
numbers: GPT-4 DAT 89.1, above 96.1% of humans; GPT-3.5-turbo 80.8, above human mean. Prompt as in Olson et al. 2021. Other open models lower, roughly in proportion to size. Top-p 0.9, temperature 0.7 helped non-GPT-4 models.
quote: GPT-4 outperforms 96% of humans, while GPT-3.5-turbo exceeds the average human level.
limits: DAT score correlates with word rarity (surprisal); the authors control for surprisal in an appendix. DAT measures divergent association, not creative usefulness. Greedy decoding on one run.
agent_relevance: Raw semantic distance is not scarce in strong LLMs. Our agent can reach far seeds cheaply; the problem is picking the useful ones.

source: Abramski, Improta, Rossetti and Stella (2025) The LLM World of Words English free association norms, Scientific Data
finding: Free-association networks from three LLMs differ strongly from human ones in diversity of answers, though priming validation looks the same. Claude Haiku has the narrowest vocabulary.
numbers: 11,545 cues, 100 prompts each, 3 answers. Unique responses: Humans 116,640; Mistral 41,369; Llama3 105,367; Haiku 15,275. Avg degree: Humans 26.1, Mistral 19.6, Llama3 28.1, Haiku 8.3. Share of human edges missing: 69%, 70%, 84%. Priming effect size 0.870 humans vs 0.859 / 0.869 / 0.866 LLMs.
limits: No ASPL, clustering or modularity reported. Nonsense responses remain. Only 50 prime-target pairs for validation. Human data cannot be redistributed.
agent_relevance: Instruction-tuned models give narrower associations than people (Haiku most so). Seed distance cannot come from the model's own free association alone; use sampling or external seeds.

source: Schiekiera et al. (2026) From Associations to Activations: Comparing Behavioral and Hidden-State Semantic Geometry in LLMs
finding: Free-association behavior of 8 LLMs matches their hidden-state geometry far worse than forced-choice behavior does. Free association is a noisy readout.
numbers: 5,000 nouns, 8 models, 17.5M+ trials. RSA: forced choice r=.346 (averaged), .463 (task-aligned); free association r=.140, about .196-.199. Cross-model consensus r=.792-.802. Ridge R2 gain: +.022 forced choice, +.002 free association.
quote: FC aligns substantially more with hidden-state geometry than FA
limits: English high-frequency nouns only, models 7B-10B, correlational.
agent_relevance: If we want to control seed distance in an LLM, use embedding or forced-choice distance, not asked-for associations.

source: Olson, Nahas, Chmoulevitch, Cropper and Webb (2021) Naming unrelated words predicts creativity, PNAS
finding: Average semantic distance of 10 named words (DAT, GloVe) correlates modestly with creativity tasks. Screened data gave larger r than unscreened; the preregistered large study gave a small r.
numbers: Study 1A n=141 (57 screened): AUT originality r=0.50 screened, 0.32 full. Study 1B n=285: originality r=0.32, flexibility 0.35, fluency 0.30. Study 1C n=50 test-retest 0.73. Study 2 (preregistered, 98 countries, 8,572): shortened AUT originality r=0.13 [0.03,0.23]; problem solving r=0.16 [0.05,0.26].
limits: Strongest values from manual screening of 57 people. Scores depend on GloVe/Common Crawl. Could be gamed with rare words. Young undergraduate women in early studies. May partly reflect overinclusive thinking.
agent_relevance: Large-sample effect (r about 0.13-0.16) is much smaller than first studies (r about 0.5): shrinkage on replication. Plan for small effects.

source: Beaty and Johnson (2021) Automating creativity assessment with SemDis, Behavior Research Methods
finding: Semantic distance between prompt and response tracks human originality ratings, strongly in some studies and weakly in others. It measures novelty, not usefulness.
numbers: Latent r with human ratings: Study 1 (N=171) .91; Study 2 (N=142) .75; Study 3 (N=133, brick) .45; Study 4 (N=62) .49 creativity, .73 novelty, -.81 appropriateness; Study 4b (N=56) .73; Study 5 (N=58) .85. Additive composition r=-.37 vs multiplicative .91 (elaboration bias).
quote: a novelty metric, and not a direct line to creativity
limits: Elaboration bias persists. Gameable with random distant words. Raters may weigh cleverness. Corpus-dependent. Single-item AUT (brick) gave r=.45. Correlation with fluid intelligence inconsistent.
agent_relevance: Distance alone is novelty; keep a separate relevance check, as distance and appropriateness are negatively correlated (-.81).

source: Creative Connections: Computational Semantic Distance Captures Individual Creativity and Resting-State Functional Connectivity (2022), J Cognitive Neuroscience
finding: Semantic distance of responses from the prompt is strongly tied to human creativity ratings (r=.81 latent) and, unlike human ratings, is not tied to visuospatial intelligence. Resting-state connectivity links are partly shared.
numbers: N=175 final (186 recruited). Semantic distance - human ratings latent r=.81. Visuospatial intelligence vs human ratings r=.46, vs semantic distance r=.11 (p=.29). About 51% of voxels in weighted-degree maps overlapped.
limits: Correlational; 49% of map unexplained; mostly women; oversampled arts/music/science majors.
agent_relevance: Distance separates from general intelligence, which makes it a plausible independent control knob.

source: Semantic memory and creative evaluation (2025), BMC Psychology
finding: In individual semantic networks, fluency dominates originality prediction. Network metrics add small and sign-mixed effects.
numbers: N=106 (120 recruited). Originality via OCSAI: only fluency predicts, R2=.503, beta=.074. Frequency score R2=.398: weighted average degree beta=.368 (p=.027), clustering beta=-31.99 (p=.042). Judged originality R2=.247: eigenvector centrality beta=158.68 (p=.011), global efficiency beta=-0.25 (p=.018). Fluency vs OCSAI r=.69; global efficiency vs OCSAI r=.34.
limits: Low OCSAI scores, trait-level, no preregistration, no multiple-comparison correction visible, signs differ across outcome measures. Authors still call it replication.
agent_relevance: After fluency, structure explains little and inconsistently. Counts of ideas matter more than network shape in this data.

source: Anon (2025) A cognitive multiplex network approach to investigate mental navigation and predict high-level cognition, Behavior Research Methods
finding: Large replication-sized sample: network exploration from animal fluency predicts self-reported creative potential modestly and divergent thinking weakly. Creative people explore the periphery more.
numbers: N=479 (500 recruited, Prolific). Creative potential (ICAA): R2=.12, predicted vs actual r=.34; use of largest viable cluster r=-.19. AUT (auto-scored): R2=.03, r=.18; fraction in LVC r=-.11 (p=.01). Earlier samples N=94 and N=163 cited.
limits: Authors call R2 modest. Self-report outcome, one 2-minute task. Limits section quotes R2 0.18-0.40 which conflicts with results (.03-.16). Leave-one-out validation.
agent_relevance: Best large-N test: structure predicts AUT at r=.18 (about 3% variance). Distance/periphery is a minor lever.

source: Knowledge structure and scientific divergent thinking (2026), Journal of Intelligence
finding: Individual concept-map network efficiency correlates weakly with divergent thinking, and an experiment on knowledge format (schematic vs associative vs case) shifts originality, but network-metric omnibus tests were not significant.
numbers: Pilot N=39, Experiment 2 N=126. SDAT originality by format F=12.66, eta2=.17. Network metrics omnibus p=.050-.055. Structure-SDAT r about .20-.28. Adding structure index raises R2 by .038-.044. Mediation test not significant. PCA: one component 99.75% of variance.
limits: Non-significant omnibus tests, post hoc contrasts rely on them, the four metrics are redundant, materials differ across conditions, Chinese undergraduates, immediate test only.
agent_relevance: An intervention on knowledge format changed originality (eta2=.17), but the structure did not mediate. Prompt format may matter more than network shape.

source: Olson et al. (2021) - robustness of DAT validity with screening
finding: Study 1A screening (removing careless responders) raised r from 0.32 to 0.50 for originality; the effect is partly noise removal and partly selection.
numbers: Screened n=57 vs full n=141: flexibility r=0.51 vs 0.34; fluency 0.21 vs 0.22; appropriateness 0.34 vs 0.22.
limits: Post-hoc screening is a researcher degree of freedom.
agent_relevance: When reading effects from this literature, assume the less-screened, larger-N number is the real one.

source: Beaty and Johnson (2021) SemDis - boundary conditions
finding: Correlation between semantic distance and ratings rises when raters are told to judge novelty and falls when they judge appropriateness. A latent mix of five models reaches r=.85 with originality in study 5.
numbers: Five models: three CBOW spaces, GloVe, TASA. Study 4 GloVe r=.61 and .78; Study 5 best CBOW r=.82. Spellcheck missing caused 4.1% data loss in a prior study.
limits: Overlapping corpora among the CBOW spaces; latent models need n>100; verbal creativity only.
agent_relevance: Distance metric depends on embedding choice; use several embeddings or a latent mix when controlling seed distance.

source: Synthesis across b01, b04, b18, b19: group versus individual networks
finding: Authors of the founding study state that group networks cannot describe individual semantic networks. Later work (b04, b18, b19) moved to individual-level networks and found weaker, mixed effects.
numbers: Founding effect: ASPL 4.6 vs 3.93 at group level with 33 per group. Individual-level follow-ups: r about .18-.34 (b19), rs about -.28 (b04), only fluency significant for OCSAI (b18).
limits: Synthesis line across studies; not a formal meta-analysis. No meta-analysis exists in what was found.
agent_relevance: No pooled effect size is available. Use r about 0.15-0.3 as the working size.

source: Chen and Ding (2023) - decoding and stability
finding: Higher temperature and top-p sampling raise DAT distance for weaker models but make outputs unstable; GPT-4 greedy outputs are already high and stable, and sampling does not help it.
numbers: Sampling at p=0.9, t=0.7 raised DAT for models other than GPT-4. DAT correlates positively with token surprisal; random-word baselines scored high through rarity.
limits: DAT depends on word rarity; stochastic outputs include low scores. Models tested were 2023 era (GPT-4-0314, GPT-3.5-turbo, Vicuna, Llama variants, ChatGLM-6B).
agent_relevance: For O7, sampling temperature is one cheap way to widen seed distance, with a stability cost to guard against.

source: Abramski et al. (2025) LLM World of Words - boundary conditions
finding: Prompting each cue 100 times gave non-human distribution: Mistral repeated meta words (input, output, association); Llama3 failed to give 100 repeats for some cues; node overlap with humans 59-84%.
numbers: Missing nodes in LLM vs human: 32% (Mistral), 16% (Llama3), 41% (Haiku). LLM nodes absent from human network: 19%, 47%, 8%.
quote: there is no systematic way to remove all nonsensical responses
limits: Models were small (7-8B) apart from Haiku 3.5.
agent_relevance: Model-generated associations need cleaning and diversification before use as seed pools.

source: Anon (2022) Semantic memory search and creative ability, Communications Biology - executive-control moderator
finding: Switching during semantic search correlates with executive tasks, so creativity effects on semantic search are confounded with executive control.
numbers: Switching vs category fluency p=0.001 (FDR), letter fluency p=0.008 (FDR), backward span p=0.032, trail-making p=0.019, Stroop p=0.017 (last three uncorrected).
limits: Uncorrected for three of five.
agent_relevance: The network shape effect may be an executive-control effect in disguise; the agent has no equivalent, so it must supply control through explicit steps.

source: Domanti et al. (2026) - hypotheses and design caveats
finding: Network metrics were computed by bootstrapping 50% of nodes over 1000 iterations; with this method tiny gaps become highly significant. The authors still report effect sizes.
limits: A 0.1 difference in path length gives d=0.42 only because the bootstrap SD is small; this is not the same as an effect across people.
agent_relevance: Significance of bootstrapped group networks is weak evidence. Prefer person-level effects (r about .2).
